title: Overview
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: When you write a Java program and run it, every variable, every object, every method call consumes **RAM (Random Access Memory)**.

Understanding *how* that memory is allocated, organized, and freed is one of the most important concepts for any Java developer — both for interviews and for writing efficient, production-quality code.

title: Who Manages Memory in Java?
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: **Automatically allocated** when you create variables and objects
**Automatically freed** by the **Garbage Collector** when objects are no longer needed

title: What Gets Stored in Stack?
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: | Data Type | Stored In Stack?

| Details |
|---|---|---|
| Primitive variables (`int`, `double`, `boolean`, etc.) | ✅ Yes | Value stored directly |
| Object references | ✅ Yes | The reference (address/pointer) is stored; the object itself is in heap |
| Method frames | ✅ Yes | One frame per active method call |
| Local variables | ✅ Yes | All variables declared inside a method |

title: What Gets Stored in Heap?
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: | Data Type | Stored In Heap?

| Details |
|---|---|---|

title: Key Characteristics of Heap
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: **Larger** than stack memory
**One shared heap** per JVM instance — all threads access the same heap
Objects live until they are **garbage collected**
Managed by the **Garbage Collector**
Running out of heap memory causes: `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError`

title: Why GC Exists
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: Without GC, heap memory would fill up with abandoned objects and eventually cause the program to crash (`OutOfMemoryError`). GC eliminates the need for manual memory management.

title: When Does GC Run?
subtitle: GC is controlled entirely by JVM. You cannot force it to run on demand.
bullets: How full the heap is
Memory allocation rate
Application pause time goals
code: System.gc();   // Suggests to JVM: "Please run GC now"

title: What Makes an Object Eligible for GC?
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: An object becomes eligible for garbage collection when there are **no more active references** pointing to it from the stack (or from other reachable objects).

title: Stop-the-World Pause
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: This is why GC algorithm design is critical — minimizing pause times directly improves application **throughput** and **latency**.
code:
Application threads:  ─────────────╗  ╔─────────────────────────
                                   ↓  ↑
GC thread:                         ╔══╝  (GC completes)
                       [ PAUSE - App threads stopped ]

title: 7.1 Strong Reference
subtitle: Lifecycle: Object lives as long as the strong reference is reachable.
bullets: **Lifecycle:** Object lives as long as the strong reference is reachable.
code:
Person pObj = new Person();   // Strong reference
// GC will NOT delete the Person object as long as pObj exists and is reachable

title: 7.2 Weak Reference
subtitle: WeakReference<Person> weakPObj = new WeakReference<>(new Person());
bullets: WeakReference<Person> weakPObj = new WeakReference<>(new Person());

// Access the object (before GC runs)
Person p = weakPObj.get();   // may return the object
**Lifecycle:** Object lives until the next GC cycle. After GC runs, `get()` returns `null`.

title: 7.3 Soft Reference
subtitle: SoftReference<Person> softPObj = new SoftReference<>(new Person());
bullets: SoftReference<Person> softPObj = new SoftReference<>(new Person());
**Lifecycle:** Object may survive multiple GC cycles until heap pressure is high enough to force eviction.
**Common use case:** Memory-sensitive caches — the cache grows when memory is plentiful, shrinks automatically under memory pressure.

title: 7.4 Phantom Reference
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets:
ReferenceQueue<Person> queue = new ReferenceQueue<>();
PhantomReference<Person> phantomRef = new PhantomReference<>(new Person(), queue);
**Common use case:** Advanced resource cleanup (e.g., closing native resources after an object is GC'd).

```
title: 9.1 Young Generation
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: Every new object is **first allocated in Eden**
When Eden fills up, Minor GC is triggered
Two equal-sized spaces: **S0** and **S1**
At any given time, **one is in use and the other is empty**
code:
Eden:  [O1] [O2] [O3] [O4] [O5]
S0:    (empty)
S1:    (empty)
Old:   (empty)

title: 9.2 Old Generation (Tenured)
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: Holds **long-lived objects** that have survived many GC cycles in Young Generation
GC here is called **Major GC** (or **Full GC**)
Major GC runs **much less frequently** than Minor GC
Major GC is **more time-consuming** because:
Objects here have many references pointing to them

title: 9.3 Meta Space
subtitle: ### What Is It?
bullets: ### What Is It?
### What Does Meta Space Store?

| Data | Description |
|---|---|
| **Class metadata** | Information about loaded classes (name, methods, fields) |
| **Static (class) variables** | Variables declared with `static` — belong to the class, not objects |
| **Constants** | Values declared `static final` |
| **Method bytecode** | The compiled instructions of methods |
### Meta Space vs. PermGen (Historical Context)

| Feature | PermGen (before Java 8) | Meta Space (Java 8+) |
|---|---|---|
| Location | Part of heap | Outside heap (native memory) |
| Size | Fixed | Dynamically expandable |
| Error when full | `OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space` | `OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace` (rare) |
| Stores | Same type of class data | Same type of class data |

title: Mark and Sweep
subtitle: The foundational GC algorithm. It operates in two phases:
bullets: The foundational GC algorithm. It operates in two phases:

### Phase 1: Mark
GC traverses all **reachable objects** starting from **GC roots** (stack references, static references).
Every reachable object is **marked** as alive.
Unmarked objects are candidates for deletion.
code:
Before Mark:
Heap: [O1✓] [O2?] [O3✓] [O4?] [O5✓]
              ↑ no ref        ↑ no ref

After Mark:
Marked alive: O1, O3, O5
Marked for deletion: O2, O4

title: Mark and Sweep with Compaction
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: Eliminates fragmentation
New objects can be allocated quickly (just move the pointer)
Better cache performance (objects are contiguous)
Compaction requires moving objects, which means **updating all references** to those objects — expensive
code:
After Compact:
Heap: [O1] [O3] [O5] [                     FREE                     ]

title: Overview Comparison
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets:
| GC Type | GC Threads | Pause Time | Compaction | Best For |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Serial GC** | 1 thread | Long | Yes | Single-core, small apps |
| **Parallel GC** | Multiple | Medium | Yes | Throughput-focused (Java 8 default) |
| **CMS (Concurrent Mark Sweep)** | Concurrent | Short (mostly) | No | Low-latency apps |
| **G1 GC** | Concurrent + Parallel | Very short | Yes | Balanced (Java 9+ default) |

title: 11.1 Serial GC
subtitle: Enable with: -XX:+UseSerialGC
bullets: **Only one GC thread** does all the cleanup work
All application threads are **paused** for the entire duration
**Slow** — single-threaded is inherently slower
**Simple** — minimal overhead, good for tiny applications or single-core systems

title: 11.2 Parallel GC *(Java 8 default)*
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: **Multiple GC threads** work in parallel (count depends on CPU cores)
Application threads still **paused** during GC, but for a **shorter time**
Higher **throughput** than Serial GC
Still has Stop-the-World pause — just shorter
code:
GC Thread 1:  ════════════
GC Thread 2:  ════════════   (parallel)
GC Thread 3:  ════════════
App Threads:  ────────╗    ╔────────────
                      │PAUSE│ (shorter)
                      └─────┘

title: 11.3 Concurrent Mark Sweep (CMS)
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: GC threads run **concurrently** with application threads — most GC work happens without stopping the app
Application threads are paused for **very short periods** (only during initial mark and re-mark phases)
**No compaction** — memory can become fragmented over time
No compaction → fragmentation can lead to `OutOfMemoryError` even with free memory
code:
App Threads:  ─────────────────────────────────────────
GC Thread:    ────────╗ ╔══════════════╗ ╔════╗ ╔──────
                      │ │  concurrent  │ │    │ │
                      │ │  GC work     │ │    │ │
                      ╚═╝              ╚═╝    ╚═╝
                    (tiny   (most work   (tiny  (tiny
                    pause)  concurrent) pause) pause)

title: 11.4 G1 GC (Garbage First) *(Java 9+ default)*
subtitle: Enable with: -XX:+UseG1GC
bullets: Divides heap into **equal-sized regions** (not contiguous Eden/Old/Survivor areas)
GC prioritizes regions with the **most garbage** first
Runs **concurrently** AND **in parallel**
**Does compaction** — avoids fragmentation
code:
Heap divided into equal regions:
┌───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┐
│ E │ S │ O │ E │ S │ O │ E │ F │  E=Eden, S=Survivor, O=Old, F=Free
└───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┘
GC targets regions with MOST garbage first (hence "Garbage First")

title: Impact on Application Performance
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: App threads pause less → more time processing requests
**Throughput increases** (e.g., from 1000 to 1500 requests/minute)
**Latency decreases** (faster response times)

title: Mistake 2: Thinking Objects Are Immediately Deleted When References Are Removed
subtitle: The object stays in heap until the Garbage Collector runs (which JVM controls).
bullets: The object stays in heap until the Garbage Collector runs (which JVM controls).
code:

p = null;   // Object is ELIGIBLE for GC, but NOT immediately deleted

title: Mistake 3: Confusing Stack Overflow with Out of Memory
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets:
| Error | Cause | Memory Area |
|---|---|---|
| `StackOverflowError` | Too many nested method calls (stack is full) | Stack |
| `OutOfMemoryError` | Too many objects, GC cannot free enough (heap is full) | Heap |

title: Mistake 4: String Literal vs. String Object
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets:
System.out.println(s1 == s2);   // true  (same pool reference)
System.out.println(s1 == s3);   // false (different heap objects)
System.out.println(s1.equals(s3)); // true (same content)
```
code:
String s1 = "hello";            // String Pool (heap) — may be shared
String s2 = "hello";            // Points to SAME pool entry as s1
String s3 = new String("hello");// NEW object in heap (NOT pool)

System.out.println(s1 == s2);   // true  (same pool reference)
System.out.println(s1 == s3);   // false (different heap objects)
System.out.println(s1.equals(s3)); // true (same content)

title: Mistake 5: Assuming JVM is Platform-Independent for GC Behavior
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: GC behavior (timing, algorithms used) can vary between JVM implementations (HotSpot, OpenJ9, GraalVM) and can be tuned with JVM flags. Never assume specific GC timing in application code.

title: Mistake 6: Holding Unnecessary References (Memory Leak Pattern)
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: This is a common **memory leak pattern** in Java — static collections holding strong references prevent GC from freeing objects.

title: Commonly Asked Questions
subtitle: Conceptual Details
bullets: **Stack** — stores method frames, local variables, primitive values, and object references. One per thread. LIFO.
**Heap** — stores all objects and arrays. One shared heap. Managed by Garbage Collector.
**Young Generation** — new objects start here (Eden → Survivor S0/S1). Minor GC runs frequently here.
**Old Generation (Tenured)** — objects promoted after surviving age threshold. Major GC runs less frequently.
**Meta Space (non-heap)** — stores class metadata, static variables, constants. Replaced PermGen in Java 8. Expandable.
